newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans seek army cover as guerrilla truce ends.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans seek army cover as guerrilla truce ends.

text.p: Despite fears of renewed violence, a truce called by leftist guerrillas in the southern state of Guerrero ended quietly on Monday, with the Mexican army denying reports of rebel activity.
The month-long truce called by the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) expired on Sunday night without major incidents.
Few troops could be seen on the dirt roads of rural Guerrero, casually waving cars past military checkpoints.

Residents of this small town in the verdant hills of Guerrero state formally asked the army to maintain its makeshift camp outside town, fearful that their withdrawal might once again shatter the fragile local peace.
Town commissioner Felipe Lopez Rueda said 2,000 Tepetixtla inhabitants had signed a petition asking the army to stay.
"Tepetixtla has been calm ever since the army arrived," he said. "The people have been able to go to the fields and work."
The EPR, a four-month-old force that has attacked military targets throughout southern Mexico, called the truce to allow for unimpeded local elections in Guerrero earlier this month.

For a month, the EPR suspended its ambushes and sneak attacks on army and police targets. Then on Saturday the mysterious group defiantly announced in a communique that it would resume its armed fight, rejecting negotiations.
Local media said a state prison worker was kidnapped at an EPR roadblock on Sunday, but neither the state government nor the army confirmed the reports.
Two other reports of the EPR inflicting army casualties were apparently false, with an army press office in Mexico City saying it had no incidents to report.

The governor of Guerrero, Angel Aguirre Rivero, withdrew his offer to negotiate peace with the EPR, a proposal he had made while seeking an extension of the truce. He told reporters on Sunday he would not continue to pursue talks.
"My government will act normally and not pursue the members of the armed group," he said.
